title: How MFIs decide who gets a loan?
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
When you apply for a loan at a traditional bank, they check your credit score, your income, and your assets. But what happens when someone has none of those things? That's exactly the problem microfinance institutions (MFIs) solve — and how they evaluate borrowers is more thoughtful than most people realize.

The Problem With Traditional Credit Scoring

Credit scores were designed for people who already have financial history — a credit card, a mortgage, a car loan. For the 1.7 billion people worldwide who are unbanked, that history simply doesn't exist. A farmer in rural Kenya or a street vendor in Bangladesh isn't a bad borrower. They're just an invisible one, as far as traditional banks are concerned.

MFIs had to build a completely different system from scratch.

What MFIs Look At Instead

1. Character Over Collateral

The first thing most MFIs assess is character — not in a vague way, but through direct interviews and community references. Loan officers often visit borrowers at their homes or businesses before approving anything. They want to understand how long someone has lived in the community, what their reputation is, and whether neighbors would vouch for them.

This sounds informal. It's actually highly predictive. People who are embedded in a community have more to lose if they default — their social standing, their relationships, their ability to borrow again.

2. Business Viability

MFIs look at whether the borrower has a realistic plan for the money. A woman who wants to buy two more sewing machines to fill existing orders is a different risk than someone with a vague plan to "start a business." Loan officers are trained to ask specific questions: Who are your customers? What does one week of revenue look like? What happens if sales drop?

3. Cash Flow, Not Income

Traditional banks want to see a salary. MFIs care about cash flow — money that actually moves in and out of a business on a weekly or monthly basis. A food vendor might not have a "salary," but she can show that she consistently makes $40 on market days and has been doing so for two years. That consistency matters more than a formal income statement.

4. Group Lending Model

Many MFIs use a group lending structure where 5 to 10 borrowers form a group and vouch for each other. If one person defaults, the rest are responsible — and the entire group loses access to future loans. This creates a built-in accountability system that banks don't have. Borrowers vet each other before joining a group, which means the screening happens before the loan officer even gets involved.

How Loan Sizes Are Determined

MFIs almost always start small — sometimes as little as $25 to $100. This isn't arbitrary. A small first loan is a test. If the borrower repays on time, they qualify for a larger loan next cycle. This graduation model rewards reliability and builds trust incrementally.

A typical loan ladder might look like this:

  • Loan 1: $50 — repaid over 3 months

  • Loan 2: $150 — repaid over 6 months

  • Loan 3: $400 — repaid over 12 months

  • Loan 4: $1,000+ — with expanded business documentation

Each step up requires a clean repayment record. There are no shortcuts.

How AI Is Changing This

In markets where mobile money is common — Kenya, Bangladesh, India — MFIs are increasingly using transaction history from mobile payment apps to supplement their assessments. An AI model might analyze 18 months of mobile payment data to predict repayment likelihood with more accuracy than a human interview alone.

This doesn't replace the human judgment. It adds a layer of data that didn't exist before. The result is faster approvals, lower default rates, and access for borrowers who might have been turned away simply because a loan officer couldn't visit their village.

Why This Matters

The way MFIs evaluate borrowers reflects something important: financial trustworthiness is not the same as financial history. Millions of people around the world are reliable, resourceful, and creditworthy — they just never had a system that could see that. Microfinance built one.

Understanding how loan decisions get made is useful whether you're planning to work in this field, start a chapter, or simply think more critically about how money and access intersect in the real world.

title: Chapter Spotlight: What Actually Happens at PD's Microfinance Club
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
Spoiler: it's not just a resume line. There's pizza, real debates, and people from actual industry who show up and talk straight.

Most school clubs feel like a box to check. Show up, sign the sheet, put it on your college app. Providence Day's Kiva chapter is trying hard not to be that.

Here's an honest look at what a typical meeting looks like — and why students keep coming back.

Meetings run about an hour. No PowerPoint decks for the sake of it, no reading off slides. The structure is loose enough that actual conversation can happen.

🍕Food First

Pizza shows up before the agenda does. It sounds gimmicky but it energizes the room — conversations start flowing before we get down to business.

🧠The Think Tank

A real-world problem gets thrown on the table. Recent ones: "Should microfinance institutions charge interest at all?" and "Can AI replace loan officers in rural villages?" Students argue both sides. It gets heated — in a good way.

👔Guest Speakers — C-Suite, Not Keynote-Speak

Industry professionals come in and talk like people, not like a TED Talk. Recent meetings have featured bankers, nonprofit founders, and fintech operators. The rule: students ask the hard questions, guests answer honestly.

🤝The Hangout After

The best conversations happen after the meeting officially ends. Students stick around, swap LinkedIn connections with speakers, and continue debates that started during the think tank.

Most high schoolers' closest contact with the business world is a parent's friend who works in finance and says vague things about "working hard." PD's chapter is different in that the speakers actually talk about their experiences — deals they've closed, mistakes they've made, what they wish they'd known at 17.

The session with Mr. Berger had students debating whether algorithmic lending actually helps low-income borrowers or just makes discrimination faster. That's not a typical Tuesday afternoon conversation.

What Students Actually Get Out of It

Real financial literacy — not the textbook stuff in the elective course. Members learn how credit risk is assessed, why interest rates differ by market, and how lending decisions actually get made at an institutional level.

Public speaking under pressure — the think tank format means defending a position in front of peers and industry professionals, not just a teacher. That's a different muscle.

Direct access to professionals — speakers have included bankers, fintech founders, and nonprofit lending officers. Students who ask good questions walk away with LinkedIn connections that have actual context behind them.

Career clarity — members have gone on to internships in community banking, impact investing, and financial consulting. Several have used chapter experience to land positions at local credit unions and CDFIs (Community Development Financial Institutions) — organizations most high schoolers have never even heard of.

That's what makes the PD chapter work. The pizza's a bonus!

title: The Phone That Replaced the Bank: How a text message app in Kenya accidentally became the most successful fina
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
In 2007, a mobile network in Kenya launched a simple feature. You could text money to anyone with a phone number — no bank account needed. They called it M-Pesa. "M" for mobile. "Pesa" for money in Swahili.

Nobody expected what happened next.

Picture this: you live in a village in rural Kenya. The nearest bank is a 3-hour bus ride away. The bus costs money you don't have. The bank requires documents you've never had. So you keep your savings under your mattress, you borrow from loan sharks at 100% interest, and you pray nothing goes wrong.

That was the reality for hundreds of millions of people across Africa and Asia. Not because they were poor managers of money — but because the system was never built for them.

"Before M-Pesa, I had to send money home by putting cash in an envelope on a bus and hoping the driver didn't lose it."

— Small business owner in Nairobi

How It Actually Works

1 You deposit cash at a local agent

Think of it like a human ATM — a corner shop, a pharmacy, anyone registered as an M-Pesa agent. You hand them cash, they credit your phone wallet.

2 You text money anywhere instantly

Type a phone number, type an amount, send. The other person gets a text confirmation. Done in 10 seconds. Works on a $20 phone with no internet.

3 They withdraw cash at their local agent

The recipient walks to any agent near them and converts the digital money back to cash. No bank. No account. No ID required in most cases.

4Your transaction history becomes your credit score

This is where it gets interesting. Every transaction you make builds a digital footprint. And now, AI reads that footprint to decide if you qualify for a microloan — in minutes.

Then AI Happened

Here's the part most people don't know. M-Pesa launched a product called M-Shwari — a savings and loan product powered entirely by an AI that analyzes your M-Pesa transaction history.

No paperwork. No bank visit. No human review. The AI looks at how often you send money, how consistent your income is, whether you pay bills on time, and makes a loan decision in 90 seconds.

There are 1.7 billion adults on earth with no bank account. Most of them have a phone. That gap — between the banked and unbanked — is exactly what mobile microfinance is closing, one text message at a time.

In Bangladesh, a similar platform called bKash now has more users than the entire country's banking system combined. In India, the government's UPI system processed over 100 billion transactions in 2023 alone — most of them micro-payments under $5.

The wild part? AI loan models in Kenya are now outperforming traditional bank loan officers on repayment prediction. The machine doesn't care if you have collateral — it cares whether you paid your electricity bill on time for the last 6 months.

What's Next

The next frontier is embedded microfinance — loans that appear exactly when you need them, inside apps you already use. Imagine you're an Uber driver in Lagos. After 100 rides, your app offers you a $50 loan to repair your car — automatically, based on your earnings history, approved before you even finish reading the notification.

That's not science fiction. It's already being tested in Nigeria, Kenya, and Indonesia right now.

The phone didn't just replace the bank. It's building a smarter one.

title: Why Do People Almost Always Pay Back Microloans? 🤔The repayment rate that shocks every banker — and what we c
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
Imagine you lend $25 to someone you barely know, with no credit check, no collateral, no bank account required. What are the odds you get your money back?

If you said "low," you'd be wrong — really wrong. Microfinance loans get paid back at rates that make traditional banks jealous. Here's why.

Wait... Isn't Lending to Poor People Risky?

That's what big banks thought for decades. They assumed that people without jobs, credit scores, or collateral were too risky to lend to. So they just... didn't.

But in 1983, an economics professor named Muhammad Yunus in Bangladesh had a different idea. He lent $27 to 42 basket weavers who couldn't afford bamboo to make their goods. They all paid him back. Every single one.

title: Leveraging Micro-Economics for Macro Impact: Why Schools Need Microfinance Curriculums
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
Microfinance education in schools builds a powerful ecosystem that drives global change. When students learn the principles of microfinance, they do not just read about economics—they actively unlock opportunities for unbanked communities worldwide.

By introducing microfinance into school curriculums or starting a student-led club, educational institutions connect classrooms directly with Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) and Non-Profit Organizations (NPOs).

The Microfinance Impact Cycle

The infographic below illustrates how school-based microfinance initiatives feed into a continuous cycle of global growth:

Key Pillars of a School Microfinance Program

1. Educational Institutions (The Launchpad)

Schools serve as the perfect incubation space for youth changemakers. Inside a microfinance club or classroom, students learn how small loans can change lives. They become thoughtful leaders, master crowdfunding tools, and set up official non-profit school chapters to raise real capital.

2. MFIs and NPOs (The Bridge)

Student clubs do not work in isolation. They collaborate directly with established field partners. By pooling fundraising capital, students act as impact multipliers, helping local loan facilitators reach people who need financial backing the most.

3. Unbanked Communities (The Ground Impact)

The ultimate goal is driving financial inclusion. The capital and awareness generated by students provide mobile and digital banking access to remote areas. This creates successful local entrepreneurs, improves daily living conditions, and directly drives women's empowerment.

4. The Global Ecosystem (The Big Picture)

When unbanked communities thrive, the entire world benefits. Local economic growth reduces poverty, which naturally lowers crime rates. Furthermore, microfinance programs frequently target eco-friendly initiatives, funding local climate action alongside financial stability.

Student Voice: Why This Matters to Us

"We always hear about global poverty in history class, but it usually feels like a problem too massive for us to fix. Joining the microfinance club changed that completely. We aren't just sending charity; we are funding a cow for a family farm or helping a woman start a weaving business. We track the micro-loans, see the money get repaid, and watch communities lift themselves up. It taught us that regular students can actually shift the global economy."

Bringing Microfinance to Your School

Starting a microfinance movement on your campus is straightforward:

  • Add it to the syllabus: Blend microfinance case studies into existing economics, business, or social studies classes.

  • Launch a club chapter: Establish a dedicated student group focused on crowdfunding and awareness campaigns.

  • Partner up: Connect with local or international MFIs to give students direct access to verified lending platforms.

By bridging the gap between student drive and global financial tools like Kiva, schools can systematically dismantle poverty—one micro

loan at a time.

title: Harvard x PD Microfinance - AI at a Crossroads: Balancing Technological Growth with Global Equity with Prof. A
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
We recently hosted Prof. Ahmad Antar from Harvard for a talk with PD Microfinance. Prof. Antar has over 15 years of experience in investment banking and is the founder of Digital Emissions, a non-profit focused on cleaner technology. He helps companies lower their digital carbon footprint, and he brought a lot of great insights on global finance and tech to our club.

It was a great session with awesome questions, and it gave us a lot to think about as change leaders.

AI is Everywhere, But the Planet Pays for It

AI is a huge part of our lives now, whether we are using it for homework or running businesses. But it currently stands at a crossroads: it can either be a catalyst for good or a culprit for environmental damage.

While AI growth is moving fast—with costs dropping and adoption happening four times quicker than the early internet—the hidden environmental costs are massive. Over $1 trillion is being poured into AI infrastructure, and all those giant servers and GPUs running nonstop require real energy and water:

  • Emissions: AI now causes 3–4% of global emissions, which is double the entire airline industry.

  • Electricity: It uses around 3% of global electricity. Running ChatGPT for just one day takes enough power to run the city of Charlotte for an hour.

  • Water: Data centers use a ton of water for cooling. Every 20 to 50 prompts you type uses about one bottle of water. Multiply that by billions of prompts, and it adds up fast.

This is a classic example of Jevons’ Paradox: as tech gets more efficient and cheaper, people use it way more, which actually drives up total consumption and climate impact.

What This Means for Microfinance and Financial Inclusion

This isn't just a tech issue—it directly impacts financial inclusion. Climate change always hits the most vulne

rable people first. Unchecked AI growth increases inequality and puts extra pressure on the exact communities microfinance supports:

  • Small farmers dealing with droughts.

  • Artisans facing rising costs.

  • Families living without stable power or clean water.

If tech grows unsustainably, microfinance ends up fighting a much bigger economic battle on the ground.

Moving Forward Responsibly

The good news is that tech can still be used for good if we build it responsibly. Combining tech, sustainability, and equity can help create smarter energy grids, better climate-risk predictions, and fairer financial tools.

As students, we don't need a lab or a startup to help. We can start small by learning basic Python, understanding the environmental side of AI, and backing community innovation like KIVA. Small choices make big ripple effects.

Thanks again to Prof. Ahmad Antar for speaking with us and helping us think about how responsible tech can strengthen the communities we serve.

title: Frostbite's Frozen Ice raises $1200
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
What an unforgettable day! Our Fall Fest was an absolute win from start to finish. The turnout was huge, the lines were out the door, and the energy was electrifying.

Watching the kids smile while enjoying their snow cones was priceless—but best of all, it was all for a great cause. In just four hours, we raised a whopping $1,200!

100% of the proceeds have already been used to support;

Coffee Farmers in Uganda: Through BRAC Uganda, we contributed to independent growers like Jackline. This funding helps them buy fertilizer and mulch in bulk to improve their crop yields and pay for their kids' school tuition.

Market Vendors in Senegal: Through VisionFund Senegal, we are backing a women's solidarity group. They are using the funds to stock local food markets and buy wholesale inventory to support their households.

Artisans Worldwide: Through Novica, we made loans to independent artists who need upfront cash for raw materials like weaving threads to sell their crafts globally.

A massive thank you to every single person who came out, supported us, and made this happen!

title: NC State funded Microloans - Policy Proposal
author: Rishi Mishra
html:
This summer, Impact Collective got to be part of North Carolina's Governor's Page Program, a program that's been running since 1973 and brings students from all over the state to Raleigh for a week inside state government.

We toured the Legislative Building, the State Capitol, and the Executive Mansion, and sat down with state officials to talk about how policy gets made — not the textbook version, the real one.

Naturally, we couldn't stop thinking about our own work. We see this problem all the time: people and small businesses with no credit history get shut out of bank loans, even when they're perfectly capable of paying one back. So all week, we were asking — what would it look like to tackle this as actual state policy?

By the end of the week, we found out, because we had to present our own proposal in front of state officials. We pitched state-funded microloans for small businesses in North Carolina's smaller counties and cities — the ones without a nearby bank or the credit history to qualify for a loan in the first place.

It was one thing to talk about access to capital in theory. It was another to stand in front of the people who actually write the state budget and make the case ourselves.

Grateful for the experience, and already thinking about what's next for this work.
